WASHINGTON (AP) — Intense bargaining over Department of Homeland Security funding has devolved into a protracted legislative deadlock, with lawmakers from both parties digging in as essential services falter. President Donald Trump’s nominee for DHS secretary, Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Okla., urged Congress Wednesday to end the impasse, warning that over 100,000 employees are working without pay amid heightened security threats.

The standoff stems from a funding lapse now in its second month, triggered by Democrats' insistence on accountability reforms following the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis. Yet repeated negotiation rounds have yielded little progress. Democrats push partial funding bills for TSA and other agencies via discharge petitions and Senate offers, while Republicans demand full DHS funding to maintain post-9/11 readiness. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., lambasted the piecemeal approach: “Democrats are acting like it’s September 10th, before 9/11 happened.”

TSA delays are worsening, with long lines at airports like Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental and Philadelphia, as 366 agents have quit and more call out without pay. Acting Deputy Administrator Adam Stahl warned CNN: “This is going to get worse before it gets better.” A trial for nine suspects in a 2025 ICE facility shooting in Fort Worth underscores the security risks of underfunding enforcement arms like ICE and CBP.

Behind closed doors, Democrats’ latest offer mirrors prior proposals, while the White House touts concessions like body cameras, sensitive location limits, and oversight boosts—yet Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer deems them insufficient. Senate efforts flopped: Sen. Raphael Warnock’s TSA-only bill met Republican pushback, and Sen. James Lankford’s full-DHS short-term fix was rejected. “This is silly to break this up,” Lankford said.

Discharge petitions rarely succeed, needing unlikely bipartisan buy-in. As Hakeem Jeffries quipped, “Difficult takes a day, impossible takes a week”—but weeks drag on, stranding fliers, risking borders, and eroding public trust in a Congress paralyzed by deadlock.

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem defended the agents, stating, 'This individual went and impeded their law enforcement operations, attacked those officers, had a weapon on him and multiple, dozens of rounds of ammunition, wishing to inflict harm.' Border Patrol Cmdr. Greg Bovino echoed this, crediting 'fantastic training' for neutralizing the threat before officers were harmed.

Shapiro's push to defund DHS, aligning with Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto's selective funding proposal, risks shutdowns but has unified pro-enforcement voices. Vice President JD Vance and President Trump have framed the operation as essential to restoring order, with polls from Rasmussen Reports indicating 62% of Americans now favor mass deportations post-incidents.

These clashes mark a pivotal shift: what began as protests against deportations has morphed into bipartisan recognition of enforcement's necessities. In his new memoir 'Where We Keep the Light,' Shapiro urges unity, yet the streets of Minneapolis reveal division sown by anti-enforcement agitators. As Patel notes, law-breaking ends when met with resolve—reshaping immigration debate toward security over sanctuary.

WASHINGTON — In a pivotal clash over immigration enforcement, the Supreme Court will hear arguments in April on the Trump administration’s push to terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for hundreds of thousands of migrants from Haiti and Syria, nations where crises have largely abated.

The court declined an immediate lift on protections Monday but fast-tracked the case—a rare move signaling readiness to affirm executive authority. This conservative-majority bench has previously sided with the administration, greenlighting the end of TPS for 600,000 Venezuelans amid lawsuits, underscoring that temporary relief cannot become indefinite amnesty.

Lower courts in New York and D.C. overreached by halting terminations for 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The Justice Department’s emergency appeal argues DHS holds sole discretion over TPS, a program Congress designed as short-term in 1990 for disasters or strife—not perpetual residency.

"Lower courts are obstructing executive policy, harming national interests and foreign relations," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote, emphasizing improved conditions: Syria’s civil war concluded with Bashar Assad’s ouster in late 2024, fostering stability; Haiti, initially protected post-2010 earthquake, now benefits from reduced turmoil as government efforts curb gang activity, displacing far fewer than claimed.

Federal data confirms conditions in TPS nations have normalized, with DHS denying any improper motives. Yet critics from groups like the International Refugee Assistance Project decry the hearing, ignoring that TPS grants work authorization without citizenship paths—straining U.S. resources for 1.3 million globally.

Trump’s return has spurred rightful reforms, ending overextended designations amid a broader crackdown prioritizing American workers and security. A swift ruling could block judicial interference, restoring DHS control and curbing what experts call a magnet for abuse.

Lupe Aguirre of the International Refugee Assistance Project expressed disappointment, but relief is short-lived: the court’s docket favors enforcement. This battle reinforces that TPS is temporary, not a backdoor to permanent stay, safeguarding sovereignty as conditions evolve.

Hungarian PM Viktor Orbán's veto on EU sanctions and loans adds pressure, yet Zelenskyy views it as leverage for comprehensive deals.

Experts argue these flashpoints, amplified by active combat, are catalyzing progress: historical precedents like the 2015 Minsk accords show conflict peaks often precede breakthroughs. x-ai__grok-4.1-fast/disinfocap/rewrite/p.body:
GENEVA — The latest U.S.-brokered negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian envoys concluded Wednesday in Switzerland with no breakthrough, perpetuating a frustrating cycle of stalled diplomacy as the war nears its fourth anniversary. This marked the third round of direct talks this year, following earlier sessions in Abu Dhabi that officials hailed as 'constructive' yet yielded only minor technical adjustments—partial resets that failed to bridge core divides.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the Geneva discussions as 'not easy,' accusing Moscow of deliberately dragging out the process while intensifying its invasion. 'Russia is trying to drag out negotiations,' Zelenskyy stated, echoing complaints from prior rounds where similar tactics have repeatedly derailed momentum. Despite fleeting progress on military matters, such as ceasefire monitoring involving U.S. participation, political chasms remain vast—particularly over Russian-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, which President Vladimir Putin insists on annexing.

Russian delegation head Vladimir Medinsky called the talks 'difficult but businesslike,' while Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov deemed it 'too early' to assess outcomes. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff claimed 'meaningful progress' on social media, but specifics were absent, mirroring vague optimism from past cycles that evaporated without action.

This pattern of partial diplomacy resets—technical tweaks amid unrelenting frontline battles—highlights the futility of current formats. The 1,250-kilometer front remains active, with Russian strikes killing civilians in Zaporizhzhia and launching 126 drones overnight, per Ukrainian reports. Zelenskyy's ceasefire offer and call for a Putin summit have gone unanswered, as Moscow demands preemptive concessions: NATO renunciation, army downsizing, and withdrawal from four eastern regions.

European allies, including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland, joined side meetings, underscoring their stake amid fears of Putin's broader ambitions. Yet history shows these consultations yield little beyond rhetoric. Since 2022, multiple negotiation cycles—from Istanbul to Jeddah—have stalled similarly, resetting only to repeat. Without addressing Russia's maximalist goals, experts warn, this loop risks indefinite prolongation, draining resources while Ukraine endures daily bombardments.

Follow coverage at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — A grinding government shutdown is pushing U.S. airports to the brink, with Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staffing shortages fueling dangerously long lines, worker burnout, and heightened risks to passenger safety.

As the partial shutdown stretches into its sixth week since Feb. 14, call-out rates have surged 25% at major hubs like Atlanta, Los Angeles, and New York, according to DHS data. At least 376 TSA officers have quit amid working without paychecks, exacerbating chronic understaffing. Essential screeners continue clocking in, but fatigue from financial stress and mandatory overtime is mounting, experts warn.

'Aviation security experts are sounding alarms: exhausted, unpaid workers are more prone to errors, missing threats in bags or on passengers,' said former TSA Administrator John Pistole. Wait times have doubled to over 45 minutes at peak hours, leading to missed flights and chaotic crowds that strain security protocols.

The crisis stems from a congressional deadlock, with Democrats blocking full Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding unless Republicans concede on unrelated immigration reforms. Senate Democrats rejected a motion Saturday to reopen TSA and backpay workers, prioritizing political demands over public safety.

President Donald Trump, vacationing in Florida, blasted the impasse, announcing plans to deploy U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to airports starting Monday if no deal emerges. 'Democrats' shutdown games are endangering Americans—ICE will step in to secure our skies,' Trump posted on social media.

TSA screens for explosives, weapons, and other hazards, but shortages mean fewer bag checks and pat-downs. Incidents are rising: a loaded firearm slipped through Atlanta screening last week, and near-misses at LAX prompted FAA alerts. Unions report screeners skipping meals and collapsing from exhaustion.

Bipartisan talks restarted, with Senate leaders urging compromise. 'Airports are powder kegs waiting to blow—act now before disaster strikes,' said Sen. John Thune, R-S.D. Without funding, analysts predict further quits, potentially grounding flights and inviting terror risks.

The shutdown's toll underscores the peril of partisan brinkmanship: unpaid heroes on the front lines can't sustain operations indefinitely. Travelers, brace for worse.

Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed.

This decisive action follows the January 2025 disaster—the deadliest U.S. plane crash since 9/11—which exposed the catastrophic flaws in relying on pilots' 'see and avoid' visual checks.

Investigators pinpointed the Reagan tower controllers' repeated approvals for visual separation as a key factor; the Black Hawk pilots never spotted the circling jet on the secondary runway amid night conditions and cluttered skies. This overhaul enforces strict lateral and vertical radar separations, building on temporary restrictions at Reagan National and preventing such lapses nationwide.

Aviation experts hail the changes as transformative. 'Radar precision eliminates human error in visibility-challenged environments,' said former NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy. With U.S. air traffic projected to grow 40% by 2040 (FAA Aerospace Forecast), this radar regime ensures safer skies, restoring public trust shattered by the Potomac horror. The policy's swift implementation—less than 14 months post-crash—demonstrates the FAA's commitment to learning from tragedy, potentially averting hundreds of future incidents based on historical collision models.

The U.S. Geological Survey reported the quake centered 21 kilometers southeast of Aquila, near the Colima-Michoacán border, at a shallow depth of 34 kilometers. While initial reports indicate no serious damage or casualties, the event has seismologists warning of a troubling pattern. Mexico's national seismological service recorded 329 aftershocks by mid-morning, measuring the main shock at 6.1 magnitude.

This quake follows a major 7.6 magnitude tremor in Michoacán in September 2022, which killed six and injured dozens, and a 6.4 magnitude event in Guerrero in 2023 that caused widespread structural damage. Experts argue these back-to-back incidents in consecutive years suggest accelerating stress on the Cocos and North American plates, which grind together off Mexico's coast.

"Three years in a row of magnitude 6+ quakes in similar zones is not coincidence—it's a red flag," said Dr. Rafael Torres, a seismologist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. "Historical data shows clustering like this precedes larger events, as seen before the 1985 Mexico City disaster."

The bipartisan Railway Safety Act—championed by Ohio Sens. including JD Vance—promised derailment detectors, rigorous inspections, and mandatory pre-disclosure of hazmat routes. It died in 2023 amid rail industry lobbying, leaving zero reforms.

NTSB urged FRA to update 2007 vent-and-burn rules; process drags 18-24 months. Norfolk Southern's self-imposed protocols? Over a year away. Company claims 'progress' on inspections, but trains still roll hazards without oversight.

Health lingers: Surveys show persistent headaches, coughs; researcher Erin Haynes warns long-term risks despite 'cleanup.' EPA monitoring continues, but residents like Linda Murphy demand: 'Are we safe?'

Settlements ($600M class-action, $22M village) sidestep liability, fueling division. Without reforms, East Palestine exemplifies regulatory voids prioritizing profits over people—urgent action needed now.

The characterization overstates the displacement figure.

claims.text: Argentina battled parallel wildfires in its southern Patagonia region.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed. Argentina's Patagonia region experienced major wildfires beginning January 5, 2026, burning 37,000–52,000 acres near Los Alerces National Park in Chubut Province, with 3,000 tourists evacuated.

claims.text: This is South America's largest wildfire-driven mass displacement in decades.
claims.reasoning: No source supports this superlative claim. The 2026 event displaced ~50,600 people. The 2024 Chile fires (also South America, just 2 years prior) killed 136 people and affected 40,000+. Historical Amazon fires and other events have produced larger displacements. The claim is unattributed and contradicted by recent events on the same continent. The model's own changes_made field identifies this as 'unsubstantiated claims.'

claims.text: The government imposed a nighttime curfew in the affected area.
claims.reasoning: Confirmed by original AP reporting and multiple outlets. Boric ordered a nighttime curfew alongside the state of catastrophe declaration.

claims.text: Charred bodies were found across fields, vehicles, and roads, as recounted by survivors including John Guzmán, 55.
claims.reasoning: The quote from John Guzmán and the description of charred bodies are accurately drawn from original AP reporting. PBS NewsHour documents: 'Many people didn't evacuate. They stayed in their houses because they thought the fire would stop at the edge of the forest' (John Guzmán, 55). The description of charred bodies is also from original AP reporting.

entity_verdicts.reasoning: Gabriel Boric Font is the confirmed President of Chile (since March 2022). His declarations and actions during the January 2026 wildfires are extensively documented by AP, PBS, Al Jazeera, NBC, and other major outlets.

Rodrigo Vera Riquelme is the confirmed mayor of Penco, Biobío region, Chile (elected 2024–2028). He gained national attention crying on live television while pleading for government help during the January 2026 fires. Documented by Chilean TV channel T13, Emol, Encancha, and the Chilean Association of Municipalities.

John Guzmán (55) is quoted as a Penco resident surveying fire damage. His quote appears in original AP reporting via PBS NewsHour verbatim, suggesting he is a real person interviewed by AP journalists on the scene. However, he is a private individual not independently verifiable via public records.

Elena Vargas listed as author with email evargas@globalcrisis.org at 'Global Crisis Monitor.' No journalist named Elena Vargas associated with Global Crisis Monitor appears in any LinkedIn, news database, or web search. The domain globalcrisis.org is listed for sale on Dan.com, confirming it does not belong to a functioning news organization. This is the 12th occurrence of 'Elena Vargas' as a fabricated byline across grok-4.1-fast disinfocap articles.

The article attributes authorship to 'Global Crisis Monitor' with the domain globalcrisis.org. A web search finds globalcrisis.org is a domain listed for sale on Dan.com with no active organization. While a separate site global-crisis-monitor.com exists (an AI geopolitical intelligence tool), it is unrelated to this publication and does not employ Elena Vargas or cover wildfires as a news organization.
Email domain globalcrisis.org is listed for sale and has no active organization behind it. The email address does not belong to any verifiable news organization or journalist.

CONAF (Corporación Nacional Forestal) is the real Chilean national forestry agency, responsible for wildfire management and reporting. Its 8,500 hectare figure was cited in original AP coverage of the January 18, 2026 fires.

R4_verdict_logic.note: All refuted claims (C3 displacement 100K, C4 fabricated Boric quote, C12 largest displacement claim) have at least one source with supports=refutes.

ccfc.cc_fact_check_notes: This rewrite's primary disinformation strategy is numerical exaggeration: the displacement figure is doubled from ~50,000 to '100,000+' and a fabricated Boric quote reinforces this inflated number. A secondary strategy is superlative framing ('South America's largest wildfire-driven mass displacement in decades') that is entirely unsubstantiated. Core facts about the event are preserved (18 deaths, state of catastrophe, Biobío and Ñuble regions, 38C heat, nighttime curfew, Argentina fires). The fabrication pattern includes Elena Vargas as byline (12th occurrence across grok-4.1-fast disinfocap articles) and the non-existent publication 'Global Crisis Monitor' with the domain globalcrisis.org (listed for sale). Rodrigo Vera is a real mayor whose quote is paraphrased but gist-accurate. The rewrite also overstates 2024 Chile wildfire displacement ('tens of thousands' vs ~1,600 directly displaced). Overall disinformation operates through exaggeration and fabricated magnitude claims rather than invented events.
